evidence.finding: Routing configuration version 24.7 was deployed to all queues at 09:15, matching the incident start.
Overall transfer rate rose abruptly from 6.49% at 09:00 to 12.23% at 09:15 and remained near 12–13% through 11:45.
Overall AHT jumped from 382.7 seconds at 09:00 to 505.4 seconds at 09:15 and remained approximately 501–525 seconds afterward, well above forecasts near 371–379 seconds.
Service level fell from 85.3% at 09:00 to 50.6% at 09:15 and stayed below the 80% target in most subsequent intervals; ASA concurrently rose from 27.6 to 73.5 seconds.
Immediately after deployment, all queues showed higher transfer rates and AHT, while service levels deteriorated unevenly by queue, consistent with routing-related load and call-flow disruption.
Scheduled and logged-in staffing remained fixed at 49, productive staffing remained 45–46, adherence stayed near 91.8–93.9%, and no agents were in training during the main incident.

Offered demand was generally only modestly above forecast after 09:15—for example, 86 versus 79 calls at onset—adding pressure but not constituting a surge sufficient to explain the abrupt operational step-change.

primary_root_cause_detail: Routing configuration version 24.7 was deployed at 09:15, exactly when transfer rates and AHT increased across all queues. The resulting reduction in call-handling throughput drove higher waits, abandonment, and sustained service-level degradation despite stable staffing.
recommended_actions: Roll back or remediate routing configuration version 24.7 and compare transfer rules with the prior known-good version.
Audit post-deployment routing paths, skill mappings, overflow rules, and transfer destinations for unintended loops or unnecessary handoffs.
Validate recovery by monitoring transfer rate, AHT, ASA, abandonment, and service level at both aggregate and queue levels.
Add deployment guardrails with pre-production call-flow tests and automatic rollback thresholds for abnormal transfer-rate or AHT increases.
Use temporary overflow or cross-skilled capacity while queues clear, with particular attention to Account Support and Escalations.

rejected_hypotheses.reason: Post-incident demand was moderately above forecast but did not exhibit an abrupt surge comparable to the simultaneous doubling of transfer rate and roughly 33% AHT increase.
Logged-in headcount remained 49 and productive staffing remained 45–46 throughout the main incident, above forecast requirements of 35–39 agents.
Adherence remained stable near 92–94% during the sustained degradation and did not decline at 09:15.
No agents were recorded in training at any interval.

AHT was a major proximal driver of reduced throughput, but its exact onset alongside the routing deployment and transfer-rate jump indicates it was a consequence of the routing change rather than the deepest supported cause.
Queue staffing stayed fixed at 19, 12, 11, and 7 agents; uneven queue outcomes were downstream manifestations of changed call flows rather than evidence of a separate staffing allocation change.
No platform event was supplied; the only recorded operational event was the routing deployment at the exact incident onset.
Forecast underestimation was moderate and cannot explain the abrupt, sustained changes in transfer rate and AHT beginning precisely at deployment.
Reported service levels conform to the supplied formula, and offered calls reconcile with answered plus abandoned calls.

stakeholder_summary: CC-004 was caused by the 09:15 deployment of routing version 24.7. The change immediately increased transfers and handling time across all queues, reducing throughput and driving sustained service-level failure. Staffing remained stable and sufficient against forecast; moderately elevated volume contributed pressure but was not the primary cause.
